blocks.preview: Consider the following program:

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int x { 5 }; // x makes a copy of its initializer
    std::cout << x << '\n';

    return 0;
}
When the definition for x is executed, the initialization value 5 is copied into the memory allocated for variable int x. For fundamental types, initializing and copying a variable is fast.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    std::string s{ "Hello, world!" }; // s makes a copy of its initializer
    std::cout << s << '\n';

    return 0;
}
When s is initialized, the C-style string literal "Hello, world!" is copied into memory allocated for std::string s. Unlike fundamental types, initializing and copying a std::string is slow.

blocks.html: In the above program, all we do with s is print the value to the console, and then s is destroyed. We’ve essentially made a copy of “Hello, world!” just to print and then destroy that copy. That’s inefficient.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

void printString(std::string str) // str makes a copy of its initializer

This example makes two copies of the C-style string “Hello, world!”: one when we initialize s in main(), and another when we initialize parameter str in printString(). That’s a lot of needless copying just to print a string!

blocks.title: std::string_view C++17
blocks.html: std::string_view C++17

To address the issue with std::string being expensive to initialize (or copy), C++17 introduced std::string_view (which lives in the <string_view> header). std::string_view provides read-only access to an existing string (a C-style string, a std::string, or another std::string_view) without making a copy. Read-only means that we can access and use the value being viewed, but we can not modify it.
blocks.preview: To address the issue with std::string being expensive to initialize (or copy), C

blocks.html: The following example is identical to the prior one, except we’ve replaced std::string with std::string_view.
blocks.preview: The following example is identical to the prior one, except we’ve replaced std::

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view> // C++17

// str provides read-only access to whatever argument is passed in
void printSV(std::string_view str) // now a std::string_view
{
    std::cout << str << '\n';
}

int main()
{
    std::string_view s{ "Hello, world!" }; // now a std::string_view
    printSV(s);

    return 0;
}
This program produces the same output as the prior one, but no copies of the string “Hello, world!” are made.

When we pass s to printSV(), parameter str is initialized from s. This allows us to access “Hello, world!” through str, again without making a copy of the string.

Best practice

Prefer std::string_view over std::string when you need a read-only string, especially for function parameters.

blocks.title: std::string_view can be initialized with many different types of strings
blocks.html: std::string_view can be initialized with many different types of strings
One of the neat things about a std::string_view is how flexible it is. A std::string_view object can be initialized with a C-style string, a std::string, or another std::string_view:
blocks.preview: One of the neat things about a std::string_view is how flexible it is. A std::st

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

int main()
{
    std::string_view s1 { "Hello, world!" }; // initialize with C-style string literal
    std::cout << s1 << '\n';

    std::string s{ "Hello, world!" };
    std::string_view s2 { s };  // initialize with std::string
    std::cout << s2 << '\n';

    std::string_view s3 { s2 }; // initialize with std::string_view
    std::cout << s3 << '\n';
       
    return 0;
}

blocks.title: std::string_view parameters will accept many different types of string arguments
blocks.html: std::string_view parameters will accept many different types of string arguments

Both a C-style string and a std::string will implicitly convert to a std::string_view. Therefore, a std::string_view parameter will accept arguments of type C-style string, a std::string, or std::string_view:
blocks.preview: Both a C-style string and a std::string will implicitly convert to a std::string

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

void printSV(std::string_view str)
{
    std::cout << str << '\n';
}

int main()
{
    printSV("Hello, world!"); // call with C-style string literal

    std::string s2{ "Hello, world!" };
    printSV(s2); // call with std::string

    std::string_view s3 { s2 };
    printSV(s3); // call with std::string_view
       
    return 0;
}

blocks.title: std::string_view will not implicitly convert to std::string
blocks.html: std::string_view will not implicitly convert to std::string

Because std::string makes a copy of its initializer (which is expensive), C++ won’t allow implicit conversion of a std::string_view to a std::string. This is to prevent accidentally passing a std::string_view argument to a std::string parameter, and inadvertently making an expensive copy where such a copy may not be required.

blocks.html: However, if this is desired, we have two options:
blocks.preview: However, if this is desired, we have two options:

blocks.html:
1. Explicitly create a std::string with a std::string_view initializer (which is allowed, since this will rarely be done unintentionally)
  2. Convert an existing std::string_view to a std::string using static_cast
blocks.preview: Explicitly create a std::string with a std::string_view initializer (which is al

blocks.html: The following example shows both options:
blocks.preview: The following example shows both options:

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

void printString(std::string str)
{
	std::cout << str << '\n';
}

int main()
{
	std::string_view sv{ "Hello, world!" };

	// printString(sv);   // compile error: won't implicitly convert std::string_view to a std::string

	std::string s{ sv }; // okay: we can create std::string using std::string_view initializer
	printString(s);      // and call the function with the std::string

	printString(static_cast<std::string>(sv)); // okay: we can explicitly cast a std::string_view to a std::string

	return 0;
}

blocks.title: Assignment changes what the std::string_view is viewing
blocks.html: Assignment changes what the std::string_view is viewing
Assigning a new string to a std::string_view causes the std::string_view to view the new string. It does not modify the prior string being viewed in any way.
blocks.preview: Assigning a new string to a std::string_view causes the std::string_view to view

blocks.html: The following example illustrates this:
blocks.preview: The following example illustrates this:

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

int main()
{
    std::string name { "Alex" };
    std::string_view sv { name }; // sv is now viewing name
    std::cout << sv << '\n'; // prints Alex

    sv = "John"; // sv is now viewing "John" (does not change name)
    std::cout << sv << '\n'; // prints John

    std::cout << name << '\n'; // prints Alex

    return 0;
}
In the above example, sv = "John" causes sv to now view the string "John". It does not change the value held by name (which is still "Alex").

blocks.title: Literals for std::string_view
blocks.html: Literals for std::string_view

Double-quoted string literals are C-style string literals by default. We can create string literals with type std::string_view by using a sv suffix after the double-quoted string literal. The sv must be lower case.
blocks.preview: Double-quoted string literals are C-style string literals by default. We can cre

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>      // for std::string
#include <string_view> // for std::string_view

int main()
{
    using namespace std::string_literals;      // access the s suffix
    using namespace std::string_view_literals; // access the sv suffix

    std::cout << "foo\n";   // no suffix is a C-style string literal
    std::cout << "goo\n"s;  // s suffix is a std::string literal
    std::cout << "moo\n"sv; // sv suffix is a std::string_view literal

    return 0;
}

blocks.title: constexpr std::string_view
blocks.html: constexpr std::string_view
Unlike std::string, std::string_view has full support for constexpr:
blocks.preview: Unlike std::string, std::string_view has full support for constexpr:

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

int main()
{
    constexpr std::string_view s{ "Hello, world!" }; // s is a string symbolic constant
    std::cout << s << '\n'; // s will be replaced with "Hello, world!" at compile-time

    return 0;
}
This makes constexpr std::string_view the preferred choice when string symbolic constants are needed.
